impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 for method claims directed to treating headache with anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies permits broad genus claims where the functional limitation of treatment adds nothing substantive beyond the genus of compounds.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding broad method-of-treatment patent claims, with Judge Dyk dissenting on the ground that the panel's enablement analysis for method claims is inconsistent with Supreme Court precedent and will sustain overly broad claims that undermine medical innovation. The case involved Teva's patents claiming methods of treating headache using any humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibody.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with broad method-of-treatment claims benefit from the panel's approach, which may allow genus-level method claims to survive enablement challenges more easily than composition claims, preserving valuable patent portfolios in the pharmaceutical space.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar competitors face broader patent barriers to market entry. The dissent signals ongoing uncertainty about enablement standards for method claims, creating litigation risk for companies designing around such patents.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award related to Ford's development of competing software using Versata's licensed technology.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court reversed the district court's judgment on breach of contract damages and reinstated the jury award, while affirming Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation. The case arose from Ford's development of its own manufacturing configuration software while licensing Versata's software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors benefit from the reinstatement of the jury's contract damages award and the expanded opportunity to present trade secret damages models on remand, reinforcing protections for proprietary technology shared under license agreements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that license third-party software and later develop competing in-house solutions face heightened trade secret misappropriation risk and potentially larger damages exposure, as the court broadened the permissible damages theories available to plaintiffs.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive patent and copyright license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' sufficient to allow the licensee to sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the licensee's shift to an enforcement-only business model constituted cessation of business operations triggering automatic termination of the agreement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that the exclusive license agreement between Texas A&M University and TexasLDPC conveyed all substantial rights in the asserted patents, entitling TexasLDPC to sue in its own name without joining A&M. The court also held that TexasLDPC's shift to patent enforcement did not constitute cessation of business operations that would trigger automatic termination of the license agreement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent assertion entities and exclusive licensees benefit from clarity that enforcement-focused business models do not automatically terminate license agreements, and that comprehensive exclusive licenses can confer standing to sue independently without the licensor.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potential defense based on standing challenges to exclusive licensees, and university licensors may find it harder to argue that enforcement-only licensees have ceased operations under termination clauses.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations used in digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages, preserving the jury verdict on those issues. The case involved patents related to non-uniform constellation technology used in TV broadcasting standards like ATSC 3.0.
impacts.positiveImplications: The partial affirmance of eligibility and the preserved jury verdict on infringement and damages provide significant protection for patentees holding technology incorporated into industry standards, validating damages theories for standard-essential patent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: The partial vacatur on eligibility creates uncertainty for companies implementing broadcasting standards, as some patent claims covering standard-essential technology may face renewed § 101 challenges on remand.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims reciting a communications apparatus with a coupler matching transmitter impedance to the characteristic impedance of air are invalid for indefiniteness or lack of enablement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness ruling but affirmed the final judgment of invalidity on the alternative ground of lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a). The court found that while the claims were sufficiently definite, the specification did not enable a person skilled in the art to practice the full scope of the claimed invention, particularly given the scientific impossibility issues identified in the record.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative enablement grounds even after reversing the district court's primary indefiniteness rationale, providing multiple paths to invalidate overly broad claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face risk that courts will reach enablement invalidity sua sponte or on alternative grounds, even when prevailing on the district court's primary invalidity theory.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court provided sufficient reasoning when denying a defendant's motions for Rule 11 sanctions and attorneys' fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 after invalidating the asserted patent claims under § 101, where the patentee had notice of eligibility problems from PTO rejections of related applications.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's denial of sanctions and fee-shifting, holding that the court's order lacked sufficient detail to permit meaningful appellate review. The case involved a patentee that filed suit asserting an electronic sweepstakes patent despite the PTO having rejected claims in related applications under § 101 after Alice, and the patentee having abandoned those applications without overcoming the rejections.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers seeking fee-shifting in exceptional cases benefit from heightened scrutiny of district court denials and the expectation that courts must provide detailed reasoning, particularly where patentees had pre-suit notice of eligibility problems.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face increased risk of sanctions and fee awards when asserting patents with known § 101 vulnerabilities in related applications, as courts must now more carefully explain their reasoning for denying such motions.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in awarding attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and sanctioning plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927 after dismissing a patent infringement complaint for failure to state a claim.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal without leave to amend, the award of $207,543.60 in attorney fees to Volkswagen under § 285, and sanctions against plaintiff's counsel. The court found the plaintiff had implicitly agreed not to amend its complaint in exchange for an extension, yet attempted amendment anyway, and that the proposed amended complaint was futile. The court also addressed whether counsel had independently appealed the sanctions order.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants benefit from affirmation that courts may award substantial fees and sanction counsel personally for pursuing meritless patent infringement claims, reinforcing deterrence against frivolous patent litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent plaintiffs and their attorneys face significant financial exposure, including personal liability for counsel, when filing infringement complaints that fail to adequately plead pre-suit damages notice requirements.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming crystalline forms of cabozantinib (L)-malate salts, pharmaceutical formulations thereof, and methods of treating cancer satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that the asserted claims of the Malate Salt Patents had adequate written description, upholding Exelixis's patent protection for its cancer drug Cabometyx® against generic challenger MSN Laboratories. The patents cover crystalline salt forms, formulations, and treatment methods for the blockbuster oncology drug.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmance of written description adequacy for polymorph and salt form patents, reinforcing the viability of lifecycle patent strategies that protect commercially important drug formulations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers face continued barriers to entry where branded companies hold validated salt form and polymorph patents, potentially delaying generic competition for high-value oncology treatments.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent settlement agreement's contingent payment clause tied to the outcome of an ex parte reexamination, or whether the dispute is purely a state-law contract interpretation question.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over T-Mobile's appeal concerning interpretation of the phrase 'survives the EPR' in a patent settlement agreement, finding the dispute was a matter of Texas contract law that did not necessarily depend on resolving a substantial patent law question. The court transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties negotiating patent settlements benefit from clarity that disputes over contingent payment provisions tied to PTO proceedings may be adjudicated in regional circuits under state contract law, potentially offering more predictable adjudication.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies may face uncertainty about which appellate court will resolve patent settlement disputes, complicating forum selection and litigation strategy when settlement agreements contain provisions tied to patent office proceedings.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly construed the term 'internal diameter' in patent claims directed to oil and gas float tools, and whether the jury's findings on infringement and validity were supported.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's amended final judgment finding infringement and validity of claims of the '445 patent directed to oil and gas casing float tools, and remanded for further proceedings. The case involved a dispute over claim construction of the term 'internal diameter' that was central to both infringement and validity determinations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in the oil and gas industry benefit from closer appellate scrutiny of claim construction in patent cases involving mechanical devices, potentially narrowing the scope of asserted claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the energy sector face the risk of vacated judgments and costly retrials when claim construction disputes involve terms with multiple plausible interpretations in mechanical patent claims.
